sources.locator: CS2023 Algorithmic Foundations; August 2023; material applicable to Insertion and deletion
sources.claim: Linked-list insertion and deletion rewire a bounded number of links once the target node or predecessor is known.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Once you hold the **node just before** the spot (the predecessor, `prev`), inserting or deleting in a linked list is O(1): you **rewire one or two links**, with no shifting. Insert after prev: `new.next = prev.next; prev.next = new`. Delete after prev: `target = prev.next; prev.next = target.next`. The catch is **finding** prev: deleting "the node with value X" needs a search first, which is O(n). Test the three shapes that break list code: **empty**, **one node**, and **deleting the head**.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A playlist app removes a finished lesson from the middle of a linked list. The first version sets `prev.next = None`, and every lesson after the removed one disappears too. Deleting after prev stores prev.next, links around it, then releases or abandons the removed node safely. In this lesson you'll implement, debug and test list insertion and deletion across empty, singleton and multi-node cases.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Array representation and operations**, **Singly linked representation** (nodes, head, null), and **Correctness and counterexamples**, since edge cases matter here.

sections.heading: The rule: find the predecessor, then rewire
sections.body:
```python
def insert_after(prev, value):           # O(1).
    prev.next = Node(value, prev.next)     # new node points at the old next first.

def delete_value(lst, value):             # O(n) search + O(1) rewire.
    if lst.head is None:                   # empty list.
        return False
    if lst.head.value == value:            # deleting the head.
        lst.head = lst.head.next
        return True
    prev = lst.head
    while prev.next is not None and prev.next.value != value:
        prev = prev.next
    if prev.next is None:                  # not found.
        return False
    target = prev.next
    prev.next = target.next                # link around it.
    target.next = None                     # detach (in C/C++, also free it).
    return True
```

| Case | What must happen |
|---|---|
| empty list. | nothing to delete; return False. |
| delete the head. | head moves to head.next. |
| one node, deleted. | head becomes None. |
| middle or last node. | prev.next skips over target. |
| value missing. | list unchanged. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why set target.next = None after unlinking?", "answer": "It stops anyone holding target from walking back into the list by mistake. In C and C++ you'd also free the node to avoid a leak."}
```

examples.title: Removing a lesson from the middle of the playlist
examples.situation: Deleting after prev stores prev.next, links around it, then releases or abandons the removed node safely.
walkthrough: **Bug:** `prev.next = None` cut the chain, dropping every node after the target.
**Stores prev.next and links around it:** `target = prev.next; prev.next = target.next` keeps the rest attached.
**Test:** delete Loops from Arrays -> Loops -> Recursion and a test will expect [Arrays, Recursion]; also test head, only node and missing value.
examples.result: Finishing a lesson removes exactly that lesson and keeps the rest of the playlist.

examples.title: The insert that made a loop
examples.situation: An insert_after writes `prev.next = new_node` first, then `new_node.next = prev.next`. Printing the list now runs forever.
walkthrough: The second line read prev.next after it had changed, so new_node points to itself.
The rest of the list is unreachable, and traversal loops on one node.
Fix: set new_node.next = prev.next first, then prev.next = new_node.
examples.result: Inserts keep the list intact, and traversal ends at null.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Deleting an item by value is always O(1) in a linked list.
misconceptions.correction: Only the link change is O(1). To delete by value you must first find the node and its predecessor, which is a traversal: O(n) in the worst case.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, which part of deleting Loops costs O(n)?

analogy.example: Deleting from a linked list is like **removing a person from a line holding hands**: the person before them lets go and takes the hand of the person after. If they just let go of everyone (`prev.next = None`), the rest of the line wanders off.
usefulFor: insert: new person grabs the next hand first
limitations: People can see the whole line; code must walk to find the right person.
In C, the removed person has to be shown out (freed).

recap.summary: To implement and test list insertion and deletion, find the predecessor, then rewire in O(1): connect the new node to prev.next before updating prev.next, or link prev around the target. Treat the head specially, remember searching by value is O(n), and test empty, single-node, head, middle, last and missing cases.
